title: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD)
summary: Primary ciliary dyskinesia affects cilia, the tiny hairs that clear mucus from the airways. Mucus stays in the lungs, ears and sinuses, which leads to frequent infections.
inheritance_plain: It is inherited in an autosomal recessive way: a child is affected only if they get a changed copy of the same gene (one of many linked to it) from both parents.
carrier_meaning: A carrier has one changed copy. Carriers are healthy and usually do not know they are carriers until they are tested.
disease_meaning: A person with two changed copies has PCD. Daily airway clearance and care from a specialist team help keep the lungs healthy. Some people also have organs on the opposite side, or fertility questions a doctor can discuss.
screening: A carrier test uses a blood or saliva sample. It looks for the most common changes and cannot find every possible change.
suggested_questions: Someone in my family has PCD. Could I be a carrier?
What does a test for PCD involve?
card_summary: The tiny hairs that clear mucus don't work properly. Carriers are healthy.
carrier_short: One changed copy. Healthy. Can pass the copy on.
disease_short: Two changed copies. Affects the airways, ears and sinuses; needs specialist care.
care: Specialist respiratory and ear clinics, physiotherapy, genetic counselling and family support groups.
counsellor_questions: Which carrier test is right for me?
If I'm a carrier, could my partner be tested too?
